title: The LORD Was with Joseph
summary: Sold into Potiphar’s house, Joseph prospers under God’s blessing, refuses his mistress’s advances as sin against God, and is falsely imprisoned, where the Lord remains with him.
historicalContext: Joseph was about seventeen when his brothers sold him (37:2), and he would stand before Pharaoh at thirty (41:46), so this chapter covers part of thirteen years of slavery and confinement. His buyer, Potiphar, held a court office close to the king and commanded a guard linked to the royal prison (40:3). Egyptian household lists from the first half of the second millennium name dozens of slaves, Asiatics among them, often placed in skilled indoor work, which fits Joseph’s rise from purchased servant to steward. The note that Potiphar was “an Egyptian” may point to a time when foreign rulers held power in the Delta and native officials were worth remarking on. Adultery was regarded as a grave wrong in Egypt and across the ancient Near East, and an accusation of assault by a slave against his mistress could have brought death; the milder sentence of confinement in the king’s prison stands out against that background.
literaryContext: Genesis 39 returns to Joseph after the Judah and Tamar interlude, and the two chapters are meant to be read together: Judah “went down” from his brothers and yielded at the first sight of a woman by the road, while Joseph “was brought down” to Egypt and refused a woman who pressed him day after day. The chapter is framed by matching scenes of success in Potiphar’s house (vv. 1-6) and in the prison (vv. 20-23), each announcing that “the LORD was with Joseph” and that he found favour and prospered. The covenant name of God clusters in these frames and is nearly absent from the rest of the Joseph story. Between them stands the temptation and false accusation, told three times, first by the narrator and then twice by the woman with her own distortions. The garment, used once already to deceive Jacob (37:31-33), again becomes false evidence, and the chapter ends with Joseph placed where chapter 40 will find him.
themes: God’s presence in slavery and prison
Blessing to the nations through the chosen seed
Moral purity and the law of God before Sinai

outline.title: Blessed in Potiphar’s House
outline.summary: Bought by an Egyptian official, Joseph prospers because the Lord is with him, rises to steward of the whole estate, and brings blessing on his master’s house.

outline.title: Temptation Refused
outline.summary: Potiphar’s wife repeatedly demands that Joseph lie with her; he refuses as a betrayal of trust and a sin against God, and finally flees, leaving his garment in her hand.

outline.title: Falsely Accused and Imprisoned
outline.summary: Using the garment as evidence, the woman twice accuses Joseph of assault, and her angry husband puts him in the prison where the king’s prisoners are held.

outline.title: Blessed in the Prison
outline.summary: The Lord shows Joseph steadfast love, the keeper entrusts all the prisoners to him, and whatever he does the Lord makes to prosper.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph was brought down to Egypt; and Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard, an Egyptian, bought him of the hands of the Ishmeelites, which had brought him down thither.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The story takes up the thread dropped at 37:36, where the Midianite traders sold Joseph to Potiphar. Chapter 38 interrupted that line to follow Judah, who “went down from his brethren” of his own choosing (38:1). Now the same verb returns with a different force: Joseph “was brought down to Egypt.” Judah descended by choice and drifted into Canaanite ways; Joseph was carried down against his will and, as the chapter will show, kept himself clean in a foreign land. The narrator wants the two brothers read side by side.

Potiphar is described three ways. He is an “officer of Pharaoh,” a member of the royal court; he is “captain of the guard,” literally chief of the slaughterers, a title that may once have belonged to the king’s butchers but came to mean the commander of a bodyguard or of executioners, and later chapters connect his office with the prison for the king’s offenders (40:3-4); and he is “an Egyptian.” That last detail seems needless in Egypt, which is why it may be significant. If foreign rulers then held power in the north of the country, a native Egyptian in high office was worth noting. His name, like that of Joseph’s later father-in-law Potipherah (41:45), most likely means “the one whom Ra has given.”

The verse repeats that the Ishmaelites “had brought him down thither.” Joseph is passed from hand to hand like merchandise, and the bill of sale is all that the human eye can see. Yet the buyer is a man who stands near the throne, and the house Joseph enters is a step on the road to Pharaoh’s court. The psalmist reads the event from heaven’s side: God “sent a man before them, even Joseph, who was sold for a servant” (Psalm 105:17). Stephen sums up the chapter in one line: the patriarchs sold Joseph into Egypt, “but God was with him” (Acts 7:9).

wordNotes.term: הוּרַד (hurad) — was brought down
wordNotes.explanation: A passive causative form of yarad, “to go down.” Joseph does not go down; he is taken down by others. The simple active form described Judah’s free descent from his brothers in 38:1, so the contrast between the chapters is built into the grammar. Going down to Egypt is a recurring movement in Genesis (12:10; 46:3-4), and God later promises Jacob that he will go down with him there.

wordNotes.term: סְרִיס פַּרְעֹה שַׂר הַטַּבָּחִים (seris par‘oh sar hattabbachim) — an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard
wordNotes.explanation: Saris can mean a eunuch, but in early texts it often names a court official without that sense, and Potiphar is married. Sar hattabbachim is literally “chief of the slaughterers”; the same title is given to Nebuzaradan, the Babylonian commander who carried out Jerusalem’s destruction (2 Kings 25:8). In Joseph’s story it designates the officer responsible for the royal guard and its prison.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man; and he was in the house of his master the Egyptian.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the LORD was with Joseph.” Before any detail of Joseph’s work, the narrator gives the reason for everything that follows. This is the first time the sentence is spoken of Joseph, and it will be repeated at the turning points of the chapter (vv. 3, 21, 23). The covenant name, the LORD, is used here with unusual concentration; outside this chapter it scarcely appears in the narrative of Joseph’s life. Chapter 39 is the place where the narrator lifts the curtain and tells the reader plainly who is directing events that the characters themselves experience only as slavery, temptation, slander, and prison.

The sentence carries the promises of the earlier patriarchs into the next generation. God told Isaac, “I will be with thee, and will bless thee” (26:3), and he told Jacob at Bethel, “I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest” (28:15). Jacob had to leave the land to learn the truth of that promise in Haran; his son learns it farther away still, in Egypt, without family, freedom, or the coat that marked him as favoured. God’s presence is not bound to Canaan or to comfortable circumstances.

The result is that Joseph “was a prosperous man.” The Hebrew describes someone whose undertakings succeed, who brings tasks to a good outcome. It does not promise wealth to the godly; Joseph owns nothing, not even himself. The verse closes on that sober fact: “he was in the house of his master the Egyptian.” The presence of God and the condition of slavery stand in the same sentence. Even so, the location is itself a mark of favour. Household slaves were usually given skilled and trusted work, while others laboured in the fields, and Joseph’s place in the house puts him within sight of his master and, later, within reach of his master’s wife.

The New Testament gathers this truth into the name Immanuel, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23), and into Christ’s promise, “I am with you alway” (Matthew 28:20). The believer who finds himself in a place he did not choose may take the measure of his situation from this verse before he takes it from his circumstances.

wordNotes.term: וַיְהִי יְהוָה אֶת־יוֹסֵף (vayehi YHWH ’et-Yosef) — and the LORD was with Joseph
wordNotes.explanation: The formula of divine presence links Joseph to the promises given to Isaac and Jacob (26:24; 28:15). It is the narrator’s statement, made four times in this chapter (vv. 2, 3, 21, 23), and it uses the covenant name rather than the general word for God. The same assurance is later given to Joshua as he takes up Moses’ work (Joshua 1:5).

wordNotes.term: אִישׁ מַצְלִיחַ (’ish matsliach) — a prosperous man
wordNotes.explanation: Matsliach is a causative participle of tsalach, “to succeed, to go well.” It describes effective accomplishment more than riches; Abraham’s servant uses it of God making his journey succeed (24:21, 40). Here Joseph is the “successful man,” but verse 3 clarifies that it is the LORD who causes the success. Psalm 1:3 uses the same verb of the righteous man whose work prospers.

verses.bibleText: And his master saw that the LORD was with him, and that the LORD made all that he did to prosper in his hand.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“His master saw that the LORD was with him.” An Egyptian who served other gods recognized the hand of Joseph’s God. The text does not say how, but the most natural reading is that Joseph did not hide the source of his success. Later he will twice refuse credit for interpreting dreams and point instead to God (40:8; 41:16), and he likely spoke the same way in Potiphar’s house. Results alone might have been put down to a clever slave; it took Joseph’s testimony to connect the results with the LORD.

The witness also came through the quality of the work. Joseph’s situation gave him every excuse for sullen, minimal effort, yet whatever was placed “in his hand” flourished. That phrase, “in his hand,” becomes a thread through the chapter (vv. 3, 4, 6, 8, 22, 23) and will be sharply reversed when his garment is left “in her hand” (v. 12). Earlier outsiders made similar confessions about the patriarchs: Abimelech told Isaac, “We saw certainly that the LORD was with thee” (26:28), and Laban admitted that he had been blessed for Jacob’s sake (30:27).

Paul tells servants to work “as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Colossians 3:23), and Jesus speaks of good works that lead onlookers to glorify the Father (Matthew 5:16). Joseph, without those words, lived them in an Egyptian household.

wordNotes.term: מַצְלִיחַ בְּיָדוֹ (matsliach beyado) — made to prosper in his hand
wordNotes.explanation: The subject of the participle is now the LORD: he causes all that Joseph does to succeed. “In his hand” means under his management or control, as when Abram’s servant took his master’s goods “in his hand” (24:10). The repetition of “hand” through the chapter traces Joseph’s rise, and the phrase returns in the prison scene (v. 23). Nehemiah prays in similar terms that God would prosper his servant (Nehemiah 1:11).

verses.bibleText: And Joseph found grace in his sight, and he served him: and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Three steps mark Joseph’s rise. First, he “found grace in his sight,” the favour that a superior extends to someone beneath him. Second, “he served him,” which means more than ordinary slave labour; the verb is used for personal attendance on a master, as Joshua was Moses’ minister (Exodus 24:13) and Elisha ministered to Elijah (1 Kings 19:21). Joseph moved from the general body of servants to the master’s side. Third, Potiphar “made him overseer over his house,” placing the whole estate under his administration.

The progression shows how God usually works in this chapter. No angel appears, no voice speaks to Potiphar, no miracle forces his hand. Divine favour operates through the ordinary means of trust earned over time, and Joseph’s diligence is the channel through which the blessing flows. A seventeen-year-old who had been betrayed by his own brothers might have given himself to resentment. Instead he learned a new language, a new culture, and the management of a great Egyptian household, and he did the work well.

That apprenticeship had a purpose that Joseph could not yet see. The young man who now oversees Potiphar’s house will one day hear Pharaoh say, “Thou shalt be over my house” (41:40), and will administer the food supply of a nation. Jesus states the principle: “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10). God was preparing a ruler in a slave’s quarters.

wordNotes.term: וַיְשָׁרֶת אֹתוֹ (vayshāret ’oto) — and he served him
wordNotes.explanation: Sharat describes honourable personal service to a superior, distinct from the heavy labour usually expressed by ‘avad. It is the word for Joshua’s service to Moses (Joshua 1:1) and is later used of priests and Levites ministering before the LORD (Numbers 3:6). In the prison Joseph will render the same kind of service to Pharaoh’s officers (40:4).

wordNotes.term: וַיַּפְקִדֵהוּ (vayyafqidehu) — and he made him overseer
wordNotes.explanation: The causative of paqad means to appoint someone over a charge, to put him in authority. Joseph later uses the same verb when he advises Pharaoh to appoint overseers over the land (41:34), and Pharaoh’s choice of Joseph as ruler of Egypt fulfils on a larger scale what begins here.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass from the time that he had made him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, that the LORD blessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake; and the blessing of the LORD was upon all that he had in the house, and in the field.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The blessing now reaches beyond Joseph to the household that owns him. “From the time” Potiphar entrusted his estate to Joseph, “the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake.” The timing is precise: the blessing follows the act of trust. The word “Egyptian” is pointed. A foreign household, outside the covenant family, receives the favour of Israel’s God because the chosen seed lives among them.

This is the promise to Abraham at work in miniature. God had said, “I will bless them that bless thee … and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed” (12:3). Potiphar honoured Joseph, and his house prospered. Laban had experienced the same thing through Jacob, confessing, “The LORD hath blessed me for thy sake” (30:27). The pattern will widen in the chapters ahead until Joseph’s wisdom preserves the lives of Egyptians and of “all countries” that come to buy grain (41:57). Paul calls the promise to Abraham the gospel preached beforehand, and he finds its fulfilment in Christ, the one Seed in whom the nations are blessed (Galatians 3:8, 16).

“In the house, and in the field” is a way of saying everywhere: indoor affairs and outdoor crops and herds alike thrived. The blessing is concrete and measurable, the kind of thing an Egyptian estate owner would notice in his accounts.

The verse also lends dignity to faithful work among unbelievers. Joseph did not convert Potiphar’s house to his faith, so far as we are told, yet his presence brought the favour of God upon it. Jeremiah would later tell exiles in Babylon to seek the welfare of the city where they lived, “for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace” (Jeremiah 29:7). The people of God are placed among others to be a blessing to them, and the presence of one faithful servant can change the climate of an entire household or workplace.

wordNotes.term: בִּגְלַל יוֹסֵף (biglal Yosef) — for Joseph’s sake
wordNotes.explanation: Biglal means “on account of, because of.” Laban uses the same expression when he admits that the LORD blessed him because of Jacob (30:27). God had earlier been willing to spare Sodom on account of ten righteous people (18:26, 32, with a related phrase), showing that the presence of the faithful can bring mercy on a wider community.

wordNotes.term: בִּרְכַּת יְהוָה (birkat YHWH) — the blessing of the LORD
wordNotes.explanation: Berakhah is the good that God bestows, often fruitfulness and increase. The phrase “blessing of the LORD” appears here for the first time and recurs in Moses’ promise of abundance (Deuteronomy 33:23). Proverbs states that the blessing of the LORD makes rich and adds no sorrow with it (Proverbs 10:22).

verses.bibleText: And he left all that he had in Joseph's hand; and he knew not ought he had, save the bread which he did eat. And Joseph was a goodly person, and well favoured.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Potiphar’s confidence became complete. “He left all that he had in Joseph’s hand; and he knew not ought he had, save the bread which he did eat.” The verb “left” is unusual; it can mean to abandon or relinquish, and it will return when Joseph leaves his garment in the woman’s hand (vv. 12, 13, 15). Potiphar no longer checked anything. The exception, “the bread which he did eat,” may simply mean that his only concern was what appeared at his table. It may also reflect Egyptian custom, for Egyptians would not eat with Hebrews (43:32), and the preparation of the master’s food might have been kept from a foreign slave. Joseph’s own words in verse 9, “neither hath he kept back any thing from me but thee,” supply the one other exception the household knew.

The second half of the verse turns abruptly: “And Joseph was a goodly person, and well favoured.” The two Hebrew phrases are exactly those used of his mother Rachel (29:17), and no other man in Scripture is described with this pair. The narrator mentions it here for a reason. Beauty is a gift of God, yet in Genesis it often exposes its bearer to danger, as Sarah and Rebekah found in foreign courts (12:11-15; 26:7). Joseph’s handsome appearance sets the stage for the temptation that follows.

The juxtaposition is instructive. Joseph has reached the height of his success in Potiphar’s house, trusted with everything and admired by all. The moment of greatest prosperity is often the moment of greatest exposure, when vigilance relaxes and opportunity multiplies. Scripture warns that “favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain” (Proverbs 31:30), and that the LORD looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). What will matter in the next scene is not Joseph’s appearance but the heart that governs it.

wordNotes.term: יְפֵה־תֹאַר וִיפֵה מַרְאֶה (yefeh-to’ar vifeh mar’eh) — a goodly person, and well favoured
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance.” To’ar refers to figure or shape, mar’eh to the look of the face and person. The identical pair describes Rachel (29:17); similar language is used of Abigail and of Esther (1 Samuel 25:3; Esther 2:7). The notice prepares for the woman’s desire in verse 7 and links Joseph to the mother he had lost.

wordNotes.term: וַיַּעֲזֹב (vayya‘azov) — and he left
wordNotes.explanation: ‘Azav means to leave, forsake, or let go. It is stronger than the usual “gave into his hand,” suggesting that Potiphar relinquished oversight entirely. The verb reappears when Joseph leaves his garment behind (39:12), and Scripture uses it elsewhere of a man who leaves father and mother to cleave to his wife (2:24).

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass after these things, that his master's wife cast her eyes upon Joseph; and she said, Lie with me.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And it came to pass after these things” marks a lapse of time and a change of scene. Joseph has settled into his office as steward, and the narrative now moves from the theological summary of verses 2-6 into the events that will test him. The woman is never named. She is simply “his master’s wife,” a title the narrator repeats so that the reader never forgets whose wife she is.

She “cast her eyes upon Joseph.” The idiom describes looking with desire, and the sequence of seeing and wanting echoes the first temptation, where the woman saw that the tree was pleasant to the eyes (3:6), and anticipates David on the palace roof (2 Samuel 11:2). John calls it “the lust of the eyes” (1 John 2:16), and Jesus locates adultery already in the look that covets (Matthew 5:28).

Her words are two in Hebrew: “Lie with me.” There is no courtship and no pretence of affection. She speaks as a mistress gives orders to a slave, expecting compliance. That is what made the temptation formidable. Refusal meant offending the most powerful woman in the house, the one person who could unmake Joseph’s position with a word. Compliance, on the other hand, might have seemed safe and even advantageous; a slave in favour with his mistress could expect privileges. Joseph was young, unmarried, far from home, and cut off from every person who had known his father’s God.

The placement after chapter 38 sharpens the contrast. Judah, a free man in his own country, turned aside after a woman he took for a prostitute at a single sight by the road (38:15-16). Joseph, a slave under daily pressure from a woman with power over him, will refuse.

wordNotes.term: וַתִּשָּׂא … אֶת־עֵינֶיהָ (vattissa … ’et-‘eineha) — cast her eyes
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “she lifted up her eyes.” The phrase often means simply to look up (13:10; 18:2), but with a person as its object and in this setting it expresses longing desire. Ezekiel uses lifting the eyes to idols as an image of spiritual adultery (Ezekiel 18:6), showing how the gaze can signal the heart’s allegiance.

wordNotes.term: שִׁכְבָה עִמִּי (shikhvah ‘immi) — lie with me
wordNotes.explanation: An imperative of shakhav, “to lie down,” with “with me,” a common euphemism for sexual relations. In Genesis the expression usually marks illicit or violent unions (19:32; 34:2; 35:22) and is not used of marriage. Its blunt brevity contrasts with Joseph’s reasoned reply in verses 8-9.

verses.bibleText: But he refused, and said unto his master's wife, Behold, my master wotteth not what is with me in the house, and he hath committed all that he hath to my hand;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But he refused.” The narrator puts the decision before the explanation. Joseph does not deliberate or bargain; the answer is settled before he gives his reasons. Then, in contrast to the woman’s two words, he speaks at length. He is not flirting with the temptation by discussing it. He is setting out the principles that make it impossible.

The first reason concerns Potiphar. “My master wotteth not what is with me in the house,” that is, he does not concern himself with anything under Joseph’s care, “and he hath committed all that he hath to my hand.” Joseph sees the trust placed in him as a moral obligation. A steward who would use his master’s confidence to take his master’s wife would be guilty of the vilest betrayal, and the very completeness of Potiphar’s trust made the offence greater. Joseph had every reason to think of himself as a victim; he had been sold, owned, and stripped of his rights. Yet he speaks of his master with respect and of his duty to him with seriousness.

This sense of loyalty in subordinate service is commended throughout Scripture. Paul urges servants to show “all good fidelity,” so that they may “adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things” (Titus 2:10). Joseph adorned it long before the words were written.

wordNotes.term: וַיְמָאֵן (vayma’en) — but he refused
wordNotes.explanation: Ma’en, in an intensive form, expresses a firm and continuing refusal. The same verb described Jacob’s refusal to be comforted for Joseph (37:35) and will describe his refusal to switch his hands when blessing Joseph’s sons (48:19). Elsewhere it often marks stubborn refusal to obey God (Exodus 7:14), but here it is resolute refusal to sin.

verses.bibleText: There is none greater in this house than I; neither hath he kept back any thing from me but thee, because thou art his wife: how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph’s answer builds to its climax. First he describes his authority: “There is none greater in this house than I.” Then he names the single exception: “neither hath he kept back any thing from me but thee, because thou art his wife.” The marriage bond places her outside every grant of trust Potiphar has made. Joseph treats marriage as a boundary that belongs to the husband and wife alone, the union of one flesh established at creation (2:24). Even when one partner wished to break it, he would not cross it.

Then comes the decisive question: “how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” Joseph names God last and most weightily. Every sin against another person is first an offence against the One who made both of them and gave the law that binds them. David, after his own adultery, would confess, “Against thee, thee only, have I sinned” (Psalm 51:4). Joseph sees the matter that clearly before he is tempted, which is why he stands.

The verse carries great weight for understanding God’s law. No tablets of stone had yet been given; Sinai lay centuries in the future. Yet Joseph knew that adultery was “great wickedness” and sin against God. The seventh commandment, “Thou shalt not commit adultery” (Exodus 20:14), did not create a new duty when it was spoken from the mountain. It put into permanent written form what God had already made known. Abimelech had been warned that taking another man’s wife was sin against God, and he called it “a great sin” (20:6, 9). Abraham kept God’s commandments, statutes, and laws (26:5). Paul observes that even Gentiles show the work of the law written in their hearts (Romans 2:14-15). The moral law reflects the character of God, and it was binding from the beginning.

Joseph speaks of “God” (Elohim) rather than the covenant name, perhaps so that an Egyptian could follow him. His refusal does not spring from fear of discovery, since Potiphar checked nothing, nor from prudence about his career. It springs from a relationship. The God who was with him in that house was the God he would not offend in it.

Jesus took the same commandment to the heart, showing that it governs desire as well as deed (Matthew 5:27-28), and Paul reminds believers that their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:18-20). Joseph’s strength was not self-made. Hebrews says that Christ was tempted in all points like us yet without sin, and that he gives grace to help in time of need (Hebrews 4:15-16). The same God who stood by Joseph stands by those who call on him.

wordNotes.term: הָרָעָה הַגְּדֹלָה הַזֹּאת (hara‘ah haggedolah hazzo’t) — this great wickedness
wordNotes.explanation: Ra‘ah means evil or wickedness, the moral opposite of good. Its use here echoes the evil that marked the generation before the flood (6:5) and the deeds of Er and Onan, which were “evil in the sight of the LORD” (38:7, 10). The description “great” matches Abimelech’s complaint that Abraham had nearly brought on him “a great sin” through Sarah (20:9). Adultery is treated as a grave moral evil long before Sinai.

wordNotes.term: וְחָטָאתִי לֵאלֹהִים (vechata’ti le’lohim) — and sin against God
wordNotes.explanation: Chata’ basically means to miss a mark, and in moral use to offend against a person or standard. With “against God” it defines the deed in relation to God himself. God had told Abimelech, “I also withheld thee from sinning against me” (20:6). Later Scripture uses similar language for Israel’s sins against the LORD (1 Samuel 2:25).

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, as she spake to Joseph day by day, that he hearkened not unto her, to lie by her, or to be with her.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
One refusal did not end the matter. “She spake to Joseph day by day.” The temptation became a daily siege. The Hebrew emphasizes her ongoing talk; her two-word command of verse 7 had evidently grown into persuasion, pleading, and pressure. Repetition is one of the strongest weapons of temptation, for it wears down resolve that a single assault cannot break. Delilah used that method against Samson, pressing him “daily with her words” until “his soul was vexed unto death,” and he yielded (Judges 16:16-17).

Joseph “hearkened not unto her.” He did not merely decline the act; he refused to give her words a hearing. The narrator adds two phrases: Joseph would not “lie by her, or … be with her.” He avoided even being in her company where he could help it. This was wisdom as well as resolve. Proverbs counsels the young man concerning the strange woman: “Remove thy way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her house” (Proverbs 5:8). Paul says to “make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof” (Romans 13:14). Joseph understood that the safest place to defeat temptation is at a distance from it.

The verse shows that faithfulness is often a long obedience more than a single heroic moment. Each day Joseph had to choose again, without any assurance that his choice would be rewarded or even noticed. James counsels resisting the devil with the promise that he will flee (James 4:7); for Joseph the resistance had to be renewed daily, and in the end it was Joseph who had to flee.

wordNotes.term: יוֹם יוֹם (yom yom) — day by day
wordNotes.explanation: The doubled noun expresses continual repetition, “day after day.” A similar doubled expression describes Mordecai’s daily inquiry about Esther (Esther 2:11) and the daily seeking of God by an outwardly religious people (Isaiah 58:2). Here it measures the relentless persistence of the temptation.

wordNotes.term: לִהְיוֹת עִמָּהּ (lihyot ‘immah) — to be with her
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase extends Joseph’s refusal beyond lying “by her” (’etslah) to simply being in her presence. It may serve as a further euphemism, but it also suggests that he avoided her company. Tamar’s brother Absalom uses “been with thee” of Amnon’s assault in 2 Samuel 13:20, which shows how near such language stood to the act itself.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass about this time, that Joseph went into the house to do his business; and there was none of the men of the house there within.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“About this time,” literally “on this day,” the narrator brings the long siege to its crisis. Joseph “went into the house to do his business.” The detail clears him of any careless or deliberate approach to danger. He was not seeking her out; he was doing the work entrusted to him as steward. The danger met him at the post of duty.

“There was none of the men of the house there within.” Whether by coincidence or by her arrangement, the household servants were absent. Some have supposed that a festival or public occasion drew the staff away, though the text does not say. What matters is that the usual protections of a busy household had disappeared, and Joseph was alone with the woman who had pursued him for days.

Temptation frequently comes at such moments, when no one is watching and nothing seems to stand in the way except conscience. Jesus told his disciples to “watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation” (Matthew 26:41), and Paul promises that God will not allow his people to be tempted beyond what they can bear but will with the temptation “make a way to escape” (1 Corinthians 10:13). For Joseph the way of escape was an open door.

wordNotes.term: לַעֲשׂוֹת מְלַאכְתּוֹ (la‘asot melakhto) — to do his business
wordNotes.explanation: Melakhah is the ordinary word for work, craft, or assigned task. It is used of God’s work of creation, from which he rested on the seventh day (2:2), and of the work forbidden on the Sabbath (Exodus 20:9-10). Here it underlines that Joseph entered the house to carry out his legitimate duties as steward.

verses.bibleText: And she caught him by his garment, saying, Lie with me: and he left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got him out.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Words now become force. “She caught him by his garment, saying, Lie with me.” The verb describes seizing or taking hold firmly. Her command is the same as before, but now she backs it with her hands. Joseph had no time for a speech. “He left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got him out.”

Flight here is not cowardice. It was the only safe response to a situation in which delay would have been dangerous and argument useless. Paul tells the Corinthians to “flee fornication” (1 Corinthians 6:18) and Timothy to “flee also youthful lusts” (2 Timothy 2:22). Some temptations are to be resisted by standing firm; others are to be overcome only by leaving. Joseph knew the difference. He preferred losing his garment to losing his integrity, and he left behind the evidence that would be used against him rather than stay one moment longer.

The garment ties this chapter to Joseph’s earlier story. His brothers stripped him of his coat and used it, dipped in goat’s blood, to deceive their father (37:23, 31-33). In chapter 38 Judah’s personal items, held by Tamar, exposed his guilt (38:18, 25). Now Joseph’s garment, left in a woman’s hand, will be used to accuse him falsely. Twice he has lost a garment, and twice it has become a tool of lies. The garments he loses will one day be replaced by the fine linen Pharaoh gives him (41:42), but only after the prison.

The contrast with the “hand” language of the earlier verses is striking. Everything Potiphar had was placed “in his hand” (vv. 4, 6); now Joseph’s garment is left “in her hand.” The trust that elevated Joseph is about to be turned against him through a deceit he could not have prevented.

wordNotes.term: בֶּגֶד (beged) — garment
wordNotes.explanation: Beged is a general word for clothing, used of ordinary garments and of priestly vestments alike (Exodus 28:2). It probably refers to an outer garment or wrap. The word occurs six times in this scene, and a verb from the same consonants means “to act treacherously” (Isaiah 24:16), a sound-play that suits a story in which the garment becomes an instrument of deceit.

wordNotes.term: וַיָּנָס (vayyanos) — and fled
wordNotes.explanation: Nus means to flee from danger. It is the word used of those who escaped the battle of the kings (14:10) and of Moses fleeing from the rod turned serpent (Exodus 4:3). The Greek of 1 Corinthians 6:18 and 2 Timothy 2:22 expresses the same command to flee from sexual sin.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, when she saw that he had left his garment in her hand, and was fled forth,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The verse holds the woman in a single moment: she sees the garment in her hand and realizes that Joseph has fled. Rejected desire turns quickly into something darker. The pattern is familiar from Scripture; after Amnon had forced Tamar, “the hatred wherewith he hated her was greater than the love wherewith he had loved her” (2 Samuel 13:15). Lust that cannot have its object often seeks to destroy it.

The garment she had grasped as a means of seduction now becomes, in her mind, a weapon. James traces this progression: desire conceives and brings forth sin, and sin, when it is finished, brings forth death (James 1:14-15). Her humiliation, the danger that Joseph might speak, and her wounded pride all press her toward a lie. The sentence is left incomplete in the Hebrew and runs straight into the next verse, as if her decision followed immediately on what she saw.

wordNotes.term: בְּיָדָהּ (beyadah) — in her hand
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase answers the repeated “in his hand” of verses 3-6, where everything Potiphar owned was put under Joseph’s control. Now the one thing of Joseph’s that she holds is the cloak he abandoned. The reversal shows his sudden loss of security; the same word for hand marks both his trust and his vulnerability (compare 39:22-23).

verses.bibleText: That she called unto the men of her house, and spake unto them, saying, See, he hath brought in an Hebrew unto us to mock us; he came in unto me to lie with me, and I cried with a loud voice:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Her first move is to summon witnesses. She calls “the men of her house” and gives them a story before anyone else can speak. Her words are carefully chosen. “See, he hath brought in an Hebrew unto us to mock us.” She does not name her husband; he is merely “he,” a slight that exposes her contempt for him. She sets herself alongside the servants as “us,” the injured household, and casts Joseph as “an Hebrew,” a foreigner. Egyptians held themselves apart from Hebrews (43:32), and she plays on that prejudice to turn the staff against the man who had been placed over them.

She then claims, “he came in unto me to lie with me, and I cried with a loud voice.” The cry was important. In later Israelite law, a woman assaulted where help could be heard was presumed to consent if she did not cry out, and presumed innocent if she did (Deuteronomy 22:24, 27). By saying that she screamed, she presents herself as the victim of an attack. Yet the narrator has already shown that she called out only after Joseph had fled (vv. 12-13). The cry she reports was raised to accuse, not to resist.

This is the old pattern of sin. Adam blamed Eve, and Eve blamed the serpent (3:12-13). The guilty seek to justify themselves by charging others, and the greater the guilt, the more aggressive the charge. Scripture names Satan “the accuser of our brethren” (Revelation 12:10), who misrepresents the faithful and seeks to make God’s servants appear wicked. Joseph’s story shows the accuser’s method at work in an Egyptian household: innocence is turned into guilt by a well-timed lie supported by apparently convincing evidence.

wordNotes.term: לְצַחֶק בָּנוּ (letsacheq banu) — to mock us
wordNotes.explanation: Tsachaq, from the root that gives Isaac his name, can mean to laugh, to jest, or to make sport of someone. In an intensive form it is used of Isaac “sporting” with Rebekah in a way that revealed their marriage (26:8), and of Ishmael’s mocking (21:9). Here it carries both the sense of insult and a sexual overtone; she accuses Joseph of treating the household with contempt.

wordNotes.term: עִבְרִי (‘ivri) — an Hebrew
wordNotes.explanation: The term identifies a descendant of Eber (10:21) and was first applied to Abram (14:13). Outsiders often used it of Israelites, sometimes with a tone of contempt (1 Samuel 4:6). Joseph later calls himself one stolen “out of the land of the Hebrews” (40:15).

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, when he heard that I lifted up my voice and cried, that he left his garment with me, and fled, and got him out.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Her account to the servants continues: “when he heard that I lifted up my voice and cried, … he left his garment with me, and fled, and got him out.” The order of events is reversed. In reality Joseph fled first and she cried out afterward; in her version her screams drove him away. The reversal turns his flight from sin into the flight of a guilty man caught in the act.

She also alters a single word. The narrator said that Joseph left his garment “in her hand” (v. 12); she says that he left it “with me,” or beside her. To admit that she was holding it would raise the question of why. With that small change the evidence of her own aggression becomes the evidence of his. False witness rarely invents everything; it rearranges the truth just enough to reverse its meaning.

The ninth commandment forbids exactly this (Exodus 20:16), and Proverbs warns that “a false witness shall not be unpunished” (Proverbs 19:5). The woman is never shown facing judgment in the narrative, but the God who sees in secret had witnessed every moment.

wordNotes.term: הֲרִימֹתִי קוֹלִי (harimoti qoli) — I lifted up my voice
wordNotes.explanation: Rum, in the causative, means to raise or lift. With “voice” it describes crying aloud, whether in weeping (21:16, with a related verb) or in proclamation (Isaiah 40:9). Her claim to have raised her voice matches the legal significance of crying out (Deuteronomy 22:24), but the narrator has already shown that it came after Joseph’s flight.

verses.bibleText: And she laid up his garment by her, until his lord came home.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And she laid up his garment by her, until his lord came home.” The deed was calculated. She did not throw the garment aside in a moment of passion; she kept it as an exhibit, waiting for the one person whose verdict mattered. The hours of waiting gave her time to refine her story, which she would tell differently to her husband than to the servants.

The scene recalls Joseph’s brothers bringing his coat to Jacob and inviting him to draw his own conclusion (37:32). In both cases a garment is presented as silent proof, and in both the one who receives it accepts a lie. Proverbs lists among the things the LORD hates “a heart that deviseth wicked imaginations” and “a false witness that speaketh lies” (Proverbs 6:18-19). Here both are present, along with patience in carrying out the plan.

The narrator refers to Potiphar as “his lord,” Joseph’s master. The man whose household Joseph had blessed is about to become the instrument of his downfall.

wordNotes.term: וַתַּנַּח (vattannach) — and she laid up
wordNotes.explanation: From nuach, “to rest,” in a causative form meaning to set down or deposit. It is used of laying up the jar of manna before the testimony (Exodus 16:33) and of Aaron’s rod placed before the LORD (Numbers 17:4). Here, by contrast, an object is laid aside to serve as false testimony.

verses.bibleText: And she spake unto him according to these words, saying, The Hebrew servant, which thou hast brought unto us, came in unto me to mock me:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
When Potiphar arrived, “she spake unto him according to these words,” repeating the substance of her story but adjusting it for her new listener. To the servants Joseph was “an Hebrew”; to her husband he is “the Hebrew servant,” emphasizing his slave status and the outrage of a slave daring to approach his mistress. And again she places the blame on her husband: “which thou hast brought unto us.” The fault, she implies, is ultimately his, for bringing this foreigner into the house. To the servants she spoke of being mocked as a group; to her husband she says he “came in unto me to mock me.”

The Hebrew word order makes her sentence ambiguous; it could mean that the slave came in to mock her, or that the husband brought the slave to mock her. Either way, she manages to accuse both men at once.

The narrative records no word of defence from Joseph. Whether he was given a hearing or not, the story moves directly from accusation to punishment. In this he anticipates Christ, against whom false witnesses rose up and who, “when he was reviled, reviled not again” (1 Peter 2:23). The prophet foretold the servant of the LORD who “was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7). Joseph’s silent suffering is a shadow of that greater innocence.

wordNotes.term: הָעֶבֶד הָעִבְרִי (ha‘eved ha‘ivri) — the Hebrew servant
wordNotes.explanation: ‘Eved means a slave or servant. Combined with ‘ivri, the phrase stresses both his low status and his foreign origin, the twin grounds of her appeal to Potiphar. The same phrase appears in the law concerning Hebrew servants in Israel (Exodus 21:2), where God limits their service and secures their release.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, as I lifted up my voice and cried, that he left his garment with me, and fled out.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“As I lifted up my voice and cried, … he left his garment with me, and fled out.” This is the third telling of the event, and each telling has drifted further from the truth. The narrator gave the facts (vv. 11-12); the woman gave the servants a version in which she was the victim (vv. 14-15); now she gives her husband the same version, shaped to his pride and anchored by the garment beside her.

The repetition is deliberate on the narrator’s part. It allows the reader to watch a lie being built and rehearsed, and to see what Potiphar could not see. The reader knows Joseph is innocent; Potiphar knows only what he is told. That gap between what the reader sees and what the characters see is central to the Joseph story, and it reflects the gap between God’s knowledge and human judgment. “There is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed” (Luke 12:2), and “all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do” (Hebrews 4:13). God knew the truth even when no one else in Egypt did.

wordNotes.term: אֶצְלִי (’etsli) — with me
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “beside me.” She uses the preposition rather than “in my hand,” the phrase the narrator used in verses 12-13. The same word appeared when Joseph refused to lie “by her” (’etslah, v. 10). The small change in wording conceals her own act of seizing him and makes the garment look like something dropped by a fleeing assailant.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, when his master heard the words of his wife, which she spake unto him, saying, After this manner did thy servant to me; that his wrath was kindled.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Potiphar heard his wife say, “After this manner did thy servant to me,” and “his wrath was kindled.” The narrator does not say against whom. The Hebrew leaves the object of his anger unstated, and the omission may be intentional. He may have been furious with Joseph, or with his wife, or with the situation that forced him to choose between them. Her phrase “thy servant” presses the responsibility back on him once more.

Potiphar faced an awkward choice. To side with a slave against his wife would expose her and shame his household; to accept her story meant losing the most capable steward he had ever had. Whatever he privately believed, he acted on the public accusation and did not wait to examine it. Proverbs warns that “he that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him” (Proverbs 18:13), and that the first to state his case seems right until another comes and examines him (Proverbs 18:17). No one examined Joseph’s case.

James counsels believers to be “slow to wrath: for the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” (James 1:19-20). Potiphar’s anger produced injustice, though, as the following verses show, God would overrule it for good.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּחַר אַפּוֹ (vayyichar ’appo) — his wrath was kindled
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “his nose burned,” the usual Hebrew idiom for anger, from the flush and hard breathing of rage. It describes Jacob’s anger with Rachel (30:2) and Jacob’s anger with Laban (31:36). The same idiom is used of God’s righteous anger (Exodus 32:10), but here it describes a human passion that leads to an unjust act.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph's master took him, and put him into the prison, a place where the king's prisoners were bound: and he was there in the prison.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph’s master took him, and put him into the prison, a place where the king’s prisoners were bound.” The punishment was severe and unjust, yet it was lighter than the charge might have demanded. An attempted assault by a slave on his master’s wife could have cost Joseph his life. Potiphar instead placed him in the state prison reserved for royal offenders, which seems to have been under his own authority as captain of the guard (40:3). The restraint suggests that he did not wholly believe his wife’s account, or at least that he was unwilling to destroy Joseph completely. Even this measure of leniency was part of God’s overruling hand.

The first period of confinement was harsh. The psalmist says that Joseph’s “feet they hurt with fetters: he was laid in iron” (Psalm 105:18). Later Joseph would describe the place as a “dungeon,” using the same word as the pit into which his brothers had thrown him (40:15; compare 37:24). For the second time Joseph was cast down into a pit, rejected and punished though he had done no wrong.

The verse ends flatly: “and he was there in the prison.” That plain statement describes the outcome of Joseph’s faithfulness. He had kept his master’s trust, honoured marriage, and refused to sin against God, and the result was chains. Scripture does not promise that obedience will always be rewarded in this life. Peter writes that it is commendable when someone “for conscience toward God endure grief, suffering wrongfully” (1 Peter 2:19), because Christ also suffered, leaving an example. Joseph’s path anticipates the Servant who “was numbered with the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12), though he had done no violence.

Yet the location matters. The king’s prison is exactly where Pharaoh’s officials will soon be sent (40:1-3), and it is through one of them that Joseph will come before Pharaoh. What his enemies meant for evil, God was already turning toward good (50:20). The prison was not the end of the road; it was the next stage of the journey that God was directing.

wordNotes.term: בֵּית הַסֹּהַר (beit hassohar) — the prison
wordNotes.explanation: Sohar appears only in the Joseph story (39:20-23; 40:3, 5), and its precise sense is uncertain; it may describe a round or fortified building. The narrator also calls it a place where “the king’s prisoners were bound,” using the verb ’asar, “to bind,” which fits the psalmist’s picture of Joseph in fetters (Psalm 105:18). Joseph himself calls it a “dungeon” (bor) in 40:15.

verses.bibleText: But the LORD was with Joseph, and shewed him mercy, and gave him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But the LORD was with Joseph.” The little word “but” carries the weight of the chapter. Everything that human beings could do to Joseph had been done: his brothers had sold him, his mistress had slandered him, his master had imprisoned him. None of it altered the one fact that mattered. The same refrain that announced his rise in Potiphar’s house (v. 2) now sounds in the prison. Circumstances had changed completely; God’s relation to Joseph had not changed at all.

The narrator adds that the LORD “shewed him mercy.” The word is chesed, God’s steadfast, covenant love, his loyal kindness to those bound to him. It is the first time in the Joseph story that the word is used of God’s dealings with him. Jacob had confessed that he was “not worthy of the least of all the mercies” God had shown him (32:10); now the son receives the same unmerited kindness in a place where no outward sign suggested it. An observer looking at Joseph in fetters would never conclude that he was the object of God’s steadfast love. Faith learns to read God’s heart through his word, not through the walls of the prison.

God also “gave him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison.” This is the same expression later used when God gave Israel favour in the sight of the Egyptians at the Exodus (Exodus 3:21; 11:3; 12:36). What God did for Joseph in the prison, he would do for the whole nation in its bondage. Joseph’s experience is a pattern of Israel’s, and both point to the God who goes into affliction with his people.

The Lord did not immediately open the prison doors. He was with Joseph in the place of suffering before he was with him in the place of deliverance. The years in the prison shaped Joseph into a man who could rule without pride and forgive without bitterness. Stephen sums up: God “delivered him out of all his afflictions, and gave him favour and wisdom” (Acts 7:10). The psalmist speaks for every believer who has walked a similar road: “Though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me” (Psalm 23:4). Christ’s promise is the same: “I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee” (Hebrews 13:5).

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּט אֵלָיו חָסֶד (vayyet ’elav chased) — and shewed him mercy
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “and he extended to him steadfast love.” Chesed is loyal, faithful love within a relationship, the love that keeps covenant. Abraham’s servant praised God for not forsaking his chesed (24:27), and Jacob confessed his unworthiness of it (32:10). The Psalms celebrate God’s chesed as enduring for ever (Psalm 136:1). Here it means that Joseph’s fall had not broken God’s commitment to him.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּתֵּן חִנּוֹ (vayyitten chinno) — and gave him favour
wordNotes.explanation: Chen is grace or favour, the same word used in verse 4 when Joseph found grace in Potiphar’s sight. Here the giver is explicitly God. The phrase “give favour in the sight of” returns when the LORD gives Israel favour with the Egyptians, so that they leave Egypt with silver and gold (Exodus 3:21; 12:36).

verses.bibleText: And the keeper of the prison committed to Joseph's hand all the prisoners that were in the prison; and whatsoever they did there, he was the doer of it.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The keeper of the prison “committed to Joseph’s hand all the prisoners that were in the prison.” The pattern of Potiphar’s house repeats itself. Once again Joseph rises from the lowest position to a place of trust, and once again it is “into his hand” that responsibility is placed. The prisoner becomes, in effect, the prison’s administrator.

“Whatsoever they did there, he was the doer of it.” The phrase means that Joseph directed all the activity of the prison; nothing happened there apart from his oversight. This was not a reward for good behaviour alone. It placed him in daily contact with men who had fallen from high places, prepared him for his duties toward Pharaoh’s officers (40:4), and kept his administrative gifts sharp for the far larger task ahead.

The narrative in the next chapter shows the spirit in which Joseph served. He noticed when two prisoners were downcast and asked why (40:6-7). Suffering had not hardened him; it had made him attentive to the suffering of others. Hebrews urges believers to “remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them” (Hebrews 13:3), and Jesus counts care for the prisoner as care for himself (Matthew 25:36). Joseph, himself a prisoner, became a servant to prisoners.

wordNotes.term: שַׂר בֵּית־הַסֹּהַר (sar beit-hassohar) — the keeper of the prison
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the chief of the prison house.” Sar means a commander, prince, or official; the same word is part of Potiphar’s title, “captain of the guard” (39:1), and of the titles of Pharaoh’s chief butler and chief baker (40:2). The keeper seems to have served under the captain of the guard, who later assigns Joseph to the royal prisoners (40:4).

verses.bibleText: The keeper of the prison looked not to any thing that was under his hand; because the LORD was with him, and that which he did, the LORD made it to prosper.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“The keeper of the prison looked not to any thing that was under his hand.” Like Potiphar before him (v. 6), the keeper stopped checking anything Joseph handled. The reason is stated once more: “because the LORD was with him, and that which he did, the LORD made it to prosper.” The chapter ends with the same Hebrew word for prospering that opened Joseph’s story in Egypt (vv. 2-3), and in the Hebrew sentence it is the very last word. The narrator has built the chapter as a frame, with success in the house at one end and success in the prison at the other, and the temptation and injustice in between.

The frame teaches the chapter’s central lesson. Joseph’s circumstances moved downward, from favoured son to slave, from steward to prisoner. The LORD’s presence did not move at all. The same blessing that made Potiphar’s house flourish now made the prison flourish, and the same God who stood beside Joseph when he was trusted stood beside him when he was accused. After these verses the covenant name of the LORD is scarcely heard again in the Joseph narrative until Jacob’s blessing (49:18), as if the narrator has said what needs to be said: the rest of the story will be read in the light of this chapter.

Joseph’s wait was not yet over. Two more years would pass after he interpreted the dreams of Pharaoh’s officers before he was brought out (41:1). Prosperity in the prison was not release from it. Yet the God who had made the house and the prison prosper would in his time bring Joseph to Pharaoh’s side, and through him preserve many lives (50:20).

The pattern of humiliation followed by exaltation is completed in Christ, who “humbled himself, and became obedient unto death,” and whom God “highly exalted” (Philippians 2:8-9). Those who belong to him share the same promise. The righteous man is “like a tree planted by the rivers of water,” and “whatsoever he doeth shall prosper” (Psalm 1:3), not because his path avoids prisons, but because the LORD is with him there.

wordNotes.term: יְהוָה מַצְלִיחַ (YHWH matsliach) — the LORD made it to prosper
wordNotes.explanation: The causative participle of tsalach closes the chapter, matching verse 3, where the LORD made all that Joseph did to prosper in his hand. The repetition forms a frame around the whole account. The same verb describes God’s promise to Joshua that obedience to his law would make his way prosperous (Joshua 1:8).

wordNotes.term: אֵין … רֹאֶה אֶת־כָּל־מְאוּמָה (’ein … ro’eh ’et-kol-me’umah) — looked not to any thing
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “was not seeing anything at all.” Me’umah means “anything whatever” and, with the negative, “nothing.” The keeper gave no supervision to what Joseph managed, just as Potiphar had known nothing of his own affairs (39:6). Joseph uses the same word in the next chapter when he protests that he has done “nothing” to deserve the dungeon (40:15).

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: Where is God when doing the right thing makes your situation worse?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: The Lord’s presence went with Joseph into slavery and prison, making him a blessing to others and giving him strength to refuse sin as an offence against God, even when faithfulness cost him his place.
discussionQuestions: Why does the narrator say “the LORD was with Joseph” both when he is promoted and when he is imprisoned?
How did Potiphar come to see that the Lord was with Joseph, and what does that suggest about witness through daily work?
What three reasons does Joseph give for refusing, and why does he name God last and most weightily?
How does Joseph’s refusal show that God’s moral law was known and binding before it was written at Sinai?
What do Joseph’s silence under accusation and his faithful service in prison teach about suffering for doing right?
commonMisunderstandings: God’s presence does not guarantee freedom from hardship; the same refrain describes Joseph as a slave and as a prisoner.
Fleeing temptation is not weakness or cowardice; Scripture commends it as wisdom (1 Corinthians 6:18; 2 Timothy 2:22).
The seventh commandment was not a new rule invented at Sinai; Joseph already knew adultery to be sin against God.
The chapter is more than a lesson on resisting temptation; its frame insists that God’s faithful presence carried Joseph through injustice toward a larger saving purpose.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the refrain central: the Lord was with Joseph in the house and in the prison. Joseph’s purity grows out of that relationship with God, and God’s steadfast love holds him when his integrity is rewarded with chains.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Whatever house or prison you are in, the Lord who was with Joseph is with those who trust him; choose today to honour him in your work and in your body, and leave your vindication in his hands.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God’s unchanging law and his saving presence: the moral law, including the seventh commandment, was known before Sinai, and God gives his people grace to obey it and keeps them when obedience brings suffering.
flow: Joseph, a slave far from home, experienced God’s presence and blessing in daily work.
Pressed to commit adultery, he called it “great wickedness” and “sin against God,” showing that God’s law was known before it was written on stone.
Obedience cost him his position, and he was falsely accused and imprisoned.
The Lord stayed with him and showed him steadfast love, a pattern fulfilled in Christ, the sinless One falsely condemned.
Christ offers forgiveness for every failure and power to keep God’s commandments from a renewed heart.
simpleIllustrations: A man entrusted with the keys to every room of his employer’s house is honoured by that trust; the one locked door he respects shows whether the trust was deserved.
Some fires are fought by standing firm and some by leaving the building; Joseph knew which kind he faced and ran.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you let the God who was with Joseph be with you, and resolve by his grace to honour his law even when it costs you?
cautions: Do not present Joseph’s purity as a merit that earned God’s favour; God’s presence and grace came first.
Speak of sexual sin with pastoral care, offering Christ’s forgiveness and restoration to those who have fallen.
Do not promise that obedience always brings immediate reward; Joseph’s faithfulness led first to prison.

reflectionQuestions: Do I believe the Lord is with me in the place I would never have chosen to be?
Could the people I work for see that God is with me by the way I do my work?
When temptation comes, do I measure it first as a sin against God?
Are there situations I need to flee instead of trying to stand and argue?
How do I respond when doing right brings me loss or misunderstanding?
